subject: Cooking
title: MSG: The Most Misunderstood Seasoning
description: A quick, practical guide to MSG: The Most Misunderstood Seasoning.

hook.text: MSG was vilified for decades. Science says it's safe, natural, and found in Parmesan and tomatoes.

buildup.text: Monosodium glutamate was isolated by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 from seaweed broth.

discovery.text: MSG triggers umami receptors — the fifth taste — making food taste richer, deeper, and more savory.

twist.text: 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' was based on one anecdotal letter in 1968. No study has ever confirmed it.

climax.text: FDA, WHO, and every major food authority classify MSG as safe. The stigma was always cultural, not scientific.

punchline.text: MSG is just umami in a shaker. The fear was never real.

quiz.question: What was 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' based on?
options: One anecdotal letter in 1968 — never confirmed by studies

details.summary: Chinese Restaurant Syndrome was coined from a single uncontrolled letter to a medical journal in 1968 and fueled decades of anti-MSG bias rooted partly in xenophobia. Tomatoes, parmesan, and soy sauce all contain high levels of natural glutamate — the same compound that makes MSG effective.
details.whyItMatters: The MSG myth reveals how cultural bias can distort food science for decades. Many people who avoid MSG unknowingly consume the same glutamate in Western foods daily.
takeaways: Chinese Restaurant Syndrome originated from an uncontrolled 1968 letter
Parmesan and tomatoes contain more glutamate than most MSG-seasoned food
Anti-MSG sentiment has documented roots in anti-Asian prejudice

faq.question: Where does the fear of MSG come from?
faq.answer: In 1968, a doctor wrote to the New England Journal of Medicine describing numbness after eating Chinese food, speculating MSG was the cause. Media amplified the claim. Subsequent controlled studies failed to confirm any link, but the stigma persisted for decades.

faq.question: Do common Western foods contain glutamate?
faq.answer: Parmesan cheese has 1,200 mg of glutamate per 100 grams. Tomatoes have 250 mg. Soy sauce, Worcestershire sauce, and miso are all concentrated glutamate sources. Breast milk contains free glutamate. The compound is one of the most common amino acids in food.
